hypotheses.statement: each normalization level adds one hop to the median query
latency grows with the product of fan-outs along the path
hypotheses.note: in the direction tested: latency tracks hops (ratio 2.3 vs 2.0); fan-out was not varied independently, so the multiplicative form is not tested

hypotheses.statement: normalized memory grows faster than flat with scale
hypotheses.note: both grow linearly (exponent 1.0); normalized is a constant 2.5× larger. The extra cost is a constant factor, not a higher order

hypotheses.statement: mid is within 20% of flat on latency for 80% of queries while answering all twenty
hypotheses.note: 12/20 = 60%, not 80%. The second clause holds, and flat's failures on the reverse lookups (Q17–Q19) are worse than the hypothesis anticipated. The indexed follow-up shows the premise was mis-framed: the relevant comparison is indexed against unindexed, not mid against flat

guidelines.guideline: Write the questions the graph must answer before drawing the schema, and review the schema against them.
guidelines.evidence: The experiment fixed its twenty questions before any schema was written, which is what exposed the reverse-lookup failures below. Across cases, schemas built around what applications do with entities (`action-first`: eBay and Facebook in [15], Schema.org [17]) were sustained; the one built top-down from an upper ontology first (Cyc [19]) saw limited adoption. Competency questions are the standard form of this step [4].

guidelines.guideline: Every entity that a question starts from gets its own node or an index. Folding it into a property without an index is a scan.
guidelines.evidence: Flat folds place, organisation and tag into properties. On the three questions that start from one of those (Q17 employees of an organisation, Q18 messages with a tag, Q19 people in a city) unindexed flat scans the graph: 3×, 768× and 26× the hops of mid (5×, 1,502× and 50× at 20,000), latency slope 0.8–1.1 against 0.0–0.3 for mid. Three reverse indexes costing 2 MB (on 308 MB) remove the penalty entirely: with them flat is within 20% of the best schema on all twenty questions. On the other seventeen, flat is at or below mid's cost with or without indexes.

guidelines.guideline: Reify a relation only where you need per-statement provenance or qualifiers, and budget for it: about 2× hops and latency, 2.5× memory, on every query that crosses it.
guidelines.evidence: Normalized over mid: median hop ratio 2.03 (1.7–3.0 across the twenty queries), median latency 2.3×, memory 2.4–2.5× at every scale (H1 supported). The hop ratio is true by construction; what is measured is that the cost is a constant factor, not a higher order (H3 refuted), and that the ratio survives heavy-tailed fan-in (2.04 under Zipf). The latency and memory constants are those of one Python engine; the Kùzu run in the results reports how far they move on a database. Wikidata attaches qualifiers and references to a statement instead of reifying a node [16]; Freebase's reified compound value types had no direct equivalent when the data had to move [11].

guidelines.guideline: Decide per entity between copying its values onto the records that use them (denormalised, indexed) and giving it a node with edges. Copying wins reads and loses writes in proportion to fan-in.
guidelines.evidence: With indexes, the denormalised flat schema is within 20% of the best on all twenty read queries and mid on ten. On the write path at 10,000 persons, renaming a city touches 95 person records on flat and one node on mid; renaming a tag touches 153 messages against one; moving a person or changing an employer touches 2–3 records on flat and 4–10 on mid and normalized. Under heavy-tailed fan-in the copied values sit on thousands of records (the largest tag is on 19,691 messages), so the rename cost scales with the head of the distribution. The earlier version of this guideline said "default to mid"; the indexed and write-path runs replaced that with the trade-off stated here.

guidelines.guideline: Measure at several scales, on data with the fan-in you expect, and fit the slope. A prototype cannot show which design fails, and uniform test data hides what a supernode does.
guidelines.evidence: Q18 on flat takes 2 ms at 1,000 persons and looks acceptable; its latency slope is 1.09 ± 0.02, so it grows with the whole graph. Under uniform fan-in, neighbourhood queries (Q01–Q12, Q15, Q16, Q20) have slopes within ± 0.3 of zero on every schema and only the path searches Q13 and Q14 grow with n (1.2–1.4). Under Zipf fan-in the reverse lookups Q17–Q19 grow with n on every schema (slopes 0.75–1.0), because the answer grows with n; the schema then sets the constant (mid needs 27× fewer hops than unindexed flat on Q18), not the exponent. The main run's "mid does not scale with n on reverse lookups" was an artefact of the generator.

guidelines.guideline: Record provenance on every statement from the first load.
guidelines.evidence: `provenance-per-statement` appears in three sustained cases (Google and peers [15], Wikidata [16], Gene Ontology [18]). Freebase's per-statement sourcing was optional; at migration a large fraction of its facts could not be imported because the target required a source per statement [11].

guidelines.guideline: Check quality with soft constraints that run continuously and surface violations, not with a schema that blocks writes.
guidelines.evidence: Wikidata declares constraints on properties and reports violations by bot [16]; Schema.org accepts imperfect data and lets consumers clean it [17]; Gene Ontology reasons over logical definitions to catch inconsistencies [18]; SNOMED CT classifies every release. All four are sustained.

guidelines.guideline: Cap expressivity at what stays tractable, and give consumers subsets rather than the whole.
guidelines.evidence: SNOMED CT limits itself to the EL description-logic profile so classification stays tractable, and most implementers use extracts (`expressivity-capped-for-tractability`, `subset-for-use`). Cyc's higher-order logic made inference expensive and results hard to predict, and adoption stayed limited [19].

guidelines.guideline: Obsolete terms instead of deleting them, and keep conflicting values with ranks instead of choosing one.
guidelines.evidence: Gene Ontology obsoletes with replacement pointers and versions definitions as meaning drifts [18]; Wikidata keeps contradictory values with preferred / normal / deprecated ranks [16]. Both have run for more than two decades or one decade respectively under those rules.

guidelines.guideline: Decide who edits the schema and how, and do not let the graph depend on one sponsor.
guidelines.evidence: Editorial governance appears in Gene Ontology, SNOMED CT and the corporate graphs in [15]. Freebase was sustained by a single sponsor and ended when the sponsor's priorities changed (`platform-dependency`) [11]. Governance alone is not sufficient: Cyc had it and still saw limited adoption.

guidelines.guideline: Put records touched, latency and memory on the design-review checklist, and measure them against the schema, not only the engine.
guidelines.evidence: Of the seven quality frameworks in the RQ1 matrix, none has a metric for operational cost; OQuaRE [6] names performance efficiency but scores it from structural proxies. The benchmark literature (LUBM [25], SP²Bench [26], BSBM [27], LDBC [8]) measures latency and scale but holds the schema fixed and varies the engine. Neither connects a modelling choice to its cost, which is what a design review needs. Two cautions from this study's own data: a schema-level record count predicts the in-memory engine's time well (R² 0.93) and a database's poorly (R² 0.17 on Kùzu), so the count belongs on the checklist as a work measure, and the price has to be measured on the target engine.

guidelines.guideline: When the domain is too heterogeneous for a fixed schema, discover the schema from the data and measure extraction quality as graph quality.
guidelines.evidence: Amazon's product graph treats schema discovery as a learning problem because product types and attributes change continuously (`schema-discovered-not-designed`). Grade B source: a keynote, no peer-reviewed system paper.
